items.excerpt: U.S. AI companies are reportedly buying large quantities of second-hand and out-of-print books in German-speaking countries to train large language models, with the volumes scanned and then destroyed afterward.

AI dominated the 35th International Publishers Association Congress in Kuala Lumpur, as leaders moved past the 'golly-gee-whiz phase' to concrete strategy debates over how publishers should respond to AI.

The IPA gave its 2026 Innovation in Publishing Award to two AI firms: Shimmr, whose 'Advertising as a Service' platform automates book marketing, and Ailaysa, a multilingual AI company behind the Chai Reader discovery platform.

Three AI data-analytics startups are pitching publishers on tools that target different parts of the acquisition and marketing pipeline, promising to inform instinct-driven decisions without replacing editorial judgment.

Major publishers including Hachette, Cengage, and Elsevier, plus author Scott Turow, filed suit accusing Google of willful copyright infringement for using copyrighted books to train its Gemini AI models.

Three publishers and author Scott Turow brought what Book Riot calls the most straightforward case yet against a tech company's use of books to train AI, focused on how Google sourced its training books rather than training legality overall.

A survey commissioned by AI audiobook company Spoken found listeners rated multi-voice AI narration highly against human narrators for character-driven fiction, even as overall willingness to try AI-narrated titles fell from 70% to 61% year over year.
